facts.text: Ada Lovelace was born on 10 December 1815. Her father was the poet Lord Byron and her mother was Anne Isabella Byron; Ada was their only child.
Her mother brought her up and had her taught mathematics and science, partly to keep her away from the poetic side of her father.
Lovelace used the phrase poetical science to describe her own way of thinking.
She never went to a school or a university, but she studied science and mathematics from childhood and later took a mathematics course by letter with the mathematician Augustus De Morgan.
Charles Babbage started designing his Analytical Engine in the mid-1830s. It was a programmable calculating machine that would have needed steam power.
The engine was to be given its instructions on punched cards, like the cards that controlled the patterns woven on looms designed by Joseph Marie Jacquard.
The Analytical Engine was never built; machines of this general-purpose kind were only constructed about a hundred years later.
Babbage lectured about the engine in Turin in 1840. The Italian engineer Luigi Menabrea then wrote the first account of it, in French, published in October 1842.
The scientist Charles Wheatstone asked Lovelace to translate Menabrea’s article into English, and Babbage suggested that she add notes of her own.
The translation was printed in August 1843 in Taylor’s Scientific Memoirs and carried just her initials, A.A.L. Her notes made up 41 of its 66 pages.
Her last note, Note G, showed how the engine could work out a series known as the Bernoulli numbers. Its table is often called the first computer program.
Babbage thought of computers mainly as machines that handled numbers. Lovelace’s notes went further and described what such machines might create.
Lovelace noticed that the operations set by the cards were separate from the data the engine worked on, so the engine could act on things other than numbers if they followed mathematical rules.

She suggested that if the basic relations between pitched sounds in harmony and composition could be put into such a form, the engine might compose detailed pieces of music of any length or complexity.
She also argued that the engine could not originate anything; it could only carry out what people knew how to instruct it to do.
In his famous paper Computing Machinery and Intelligence, Alan Turing called this argument Lady Lovelace’s objection and disagreed with it.
Lovelace died on 27 November 1852 at the age of 36.
In late 2015, at events in Oxford marking 200 years since her birth, a sequence of numbers produced on a simulator of the Analytical Engine was developed into a musical theme.
